guide.summary: Unit 2 is the backbone of microeconomics: demand and supply and their determinants, price elasticities (demand, supply, income, cross-price), market equilibrium and consumer and producer surplus, changes in equilibrium, and the effects of government interventions (taxes, subsidies, price ceilings and floors, quotas) and trade policy (tariffs, world price).

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.body: A change in a good's own price causes a movement along the curve (change in quantity demanded or supplied). Demand shifters: tastes, number of buyers, income (normal/inferior), prices of substitutes and complements, expectations. Supply shifters: input prices, technology, number of sellers, taxes/subsidies, expectations, prices of other goods the firm could produce. Equilibrium occurs where Qd = Qs; shortages push price up and surpluses push it down.

sections.heading: Elasticity
sections.body: Price elasticity of demand (PED) = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP (use absolute value; midpoint method uses averages as bases). |PED| > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic, = 1 unit elastic. Demand is more elastic with more substitutes, a larger share of the budget, luxury status, and more time to adjust. Total revenue test: if demand is elastic, price and TR move in opposite directions; if inelastic, in the same direction; TR is maximized at unit elasticity. On a linear demand curve, demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low prices. Price elasticity of supply rises with time and ease of increasing production. Income elasticity > 0 normal (> 1 luxury), < 0 inferior. Cross-price elasticity > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements.

sections.heading: Surplus and efficiency
sections.body: Consumer surplus is the area below demand and above price; producer surplus is the area above supply and below price. Total surplus is maximized at the competitive equilibrium (allocative efficiency). Deadweight loss is the lost total surplus when output differs from the efficient quantity.

sections.heading: Government intervention
sections.body: A per-unit tax shifts supply up (left) by the tax amount (or demand down): consumers pay more, sellers keep less, quantity falls, government earns tax revenue (tax × new quantity), and deadweight loss results. Incidence falls more heavily on the less elastic side of the market. A subsidy shifts supply right, lowers the consumer price, raises the price sellers receive, costs the government (subsidy × new quantity), and creates DWL from overproduction. A binding price ceiling (below equilibrium) causes shortages; a binding price floor (above equilibrium) causes surpluses; both create DWL. Quotas limit quantity and create DWL.

sections.heading: International trade
sections.body: If the world price is below the domestic equilibrium, a country imports: domestic consumers gain surplus, domestic producers lose, and total surplus rises. A tariff raises the domestic price toward the domestic equilibrium: imports fall, domestic production rises, consumers lose surplus, producers gain, the government collects tariff revenue (tariff × imports), and two DWL triangles appear (overproduction and underconsumption). Import quotas have similar effects, with the revenue going to license holders.

keyTakeaways: Own-price change = movement along; other factors = shift.
Elastic: TR moves opposite to price; inelastic: same direction.
Income elasticity sign: normal (+) vs. inferior (−).
Taxes fall more on the less elastic side.
Binding ceilings cause shortages; binding floors cause surpluses.
Tariffs: consumers lose, producers and government gain, DWL results.
commonMistakes: Calling a price ceiling above equilibrium 'binding'.
Confusing the slope of demand with its elasticity.
Forgetting tariff revenue applies only to imports.
Assigning tax incidence to whoever legally pays the tax.
Shifting demand when supply-side factors change.
examTips: FRQs on taxes ask for areas: CS, PS, revenue, DWL; label points on the graph.
Use the midpoint formula for elasticity between two points unless told otherwise.
Identify substitutes/complements from cross-price elasticity signs.
For tariffs, compute imports before and after.
guide.cramSheet:
**Shifters:** D (tastes, buyers, income, related goods, expectations) · S (inputs, tech, sellers, taxes, expectations)

**PED:** %ΔQd/%ΔP · >1 elastic · TR test · elastic at high P on linear D

**Other:** income (+ normal, − inferior) · cross (+ subs, − comps)

**Surplus:** CS above P under D · PS below P above S · DWL lost triangle

**Tax:** ↑P_consumer, ↓P_seller, ↓Q, revenue = t × Q₂ · less elastic bears more

**Controls:** ceiling below eq → shortage · floor above eq → surplus

**Trade:** world P < domestic → imports · tariff: ↑P, ↓imports, revenue = t × imports, DWL

practice.prompt: The market for gasoline in a country is perfectly competitive and initially in equilibrium. The government imposes a per-unit excise tax on gasoline sellers. Assume demand for gasoline is relatively inelastic and supply is relatively elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled supply-and-demand graph showing the effect of the tax. Label the price buyers pay (P_b), the price sellers receive (P_s), and the new quantity (Q_t).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Shade (describe) the area of tax revenue on your graph.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Will buyers or sellers bear more of the tax burden? Explain using elasticity.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify the area of deadweight loss on your graph.

rubric.description: Axes price and quantity; steep (inelastic) demand and flatter supply; supply shifts left/up by the tax amount.
P_b where new supply meets demand at Q_t; P_s on original supply at Q_t; Q_t less than original Q.
Rectangle with height (P_b − P_s) and width Q_t.
Buyers, because demand is less elastic than supply; buyers can't easily reduce purchases, so price rises by most of the tax.
Triangle between Q_t and the original Q, bounded by demand and the original supply curve.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The graph has 'Price' on the vertical axis and 'Quantity of gasoline' on the horizontal axis. A steep demand curve and a flatter supply curve intersect at P₁ and Q₁. The tax shifts supply up by the tax amount to S + tax. The new equilibrium with demand is at Q_t (less than Q₁) and buyers' price P_b (above P₁). Directly below at Q_t on the original supply curve is P_s, the price sellers keep (below P₁).

(b) Tax revenue is the rectangle from P_s to P_b in height and from 0 to Q_t in width.

(c) Buyers bear more of the burden. Because demand is relatively inelastic, buyers do not reduce their purchases much when price rises, so most of the tax is passed on to them: P_b rises far above P₁ while P_s falls only slightly.

(d) Deadweight loss is the triangle between Q_t and Q₁, bounded above by the demand curve and below by the original supply curve.
